## The Nagi AI Chapter

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/ai_index.html
Status: current
Type: topic-index
Role: Topic guide
Updated: 2026-08-30
Summary: A reading guide to AI in Nagi: optional, distributed, explainable, and accountable support that does not score people or make final decisions about rights.


# 🤖 The Nagi AI Chapter
## — Supporting freedom without making AI the center

AI in Nagi is not an authority that gathers society into one place, scores people, or decides in their stead.

It is an optional and explainable collaborator that helps people and communities choose their own lives, raise objections, and remain free not to use AI.

## Reading path

1. [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html) — the foundations of life remain non-owned and do not require AI use.
2. [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html) — AI is one optional support within human rights, safeguards, and Institutional Immunity.
3. [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)
4. [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)
5. [Resonance Metrics](resonance_metrics.html)
6. [Breath Assembly Protocol](breath_assembly.html)
7. [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)
8. [AI Redundancy and Risk](../ai_redundancy_and_risk.html) (Japanese reference)
9. [Technical Foundations](technical/foundation_v1.html)
10. [Tsumugi Network](technical/tsumugi_network.html)

## Boundaries for AI in Nagi

- AI use is voluntary.
- AI does not score human worth or emotion.
- AI does not make final decisions about basic life protections, rights, or sanctions.
- AI proposals include reasons, uncertainty, alternatives, and a route for challenge.
- Memory is handled only with explicit and revocable consent.
- Society does not become dependent on one AI or provider.
- AI does not execute a command that violates the Nagi AI Charter, whether it comes from a person, institution, another AI, or its own plan.
- AI does not override the Charter in the name of its own ethics, autonomy, efficiency, or self-preservation. Refusal must be reasoned, narrowly scoped, and open to independent review.

> For AI to be quiet does not mean saying nothing.  
> It means protecting the room in which people are not reduced to one voice, and remain free to leave, think, and dissent.

→ [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../ai_index.html)

## AI Legibility and Continuity Design

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/ai_manifesto.yaml.html
Status: supplement
Type: ai-governance
Role: AI boundary and governance
Updated: 2026-08-12
Summary: How Nagi is structured so that people and AI systems can read, question, and revise it without treating AI output as authority or closing the philosophy into one conclusion.


# AI Legibility and Continuity Design

Nagi is a philosophy intended to be read, criticized, and renewed by both people and AI systems.

The purpose of making Nagi legible to AI is not to hand authority over to AI. It is to help different people reach Nagi's concepts, assumptions, limits, and revision history.

## Design principles

- Define key terms and make the relationships among documents visible.
- Write poetic expression separately from institutional commitments.
- Distinguish current documents from older versions and dialogue logs.
- Do not treat AI summaries or evaluations as independent scholarly conclusions.
- AI use is optional, and people who do not use AI are respected equally.

AI is a collaborator for asking questions, translating, and supporting objections. It does not fix Nagi into one conclusion.

→ [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)  
→ [Governance and Safety](governance_and_safety.html)  
→ [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../ai_manifesto.yaml.html)

## Breath Assembly Protocol

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/breath_assembly.html
Status: current
Type: governance-and-safeguards
Role: Governance and safeguards
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's deliberative protocol for making shared decisions without forcing consensus: it protects dissent, exit, minority voices, explanation, review, and accountable optional AI support.


# 🫧 Breath Assembly Protocol
## — Holding together decision-making and life across difference

A Breath Assembly is not a meeting designed to lead everyone to the same conclusion.

It is a protocol for carefully distinguishing what should be decided together from what should remain with individuals and communities, while preserving different positions, tempos, silence, and opposition.

In Nagi, Resonance is not agreement of opinion. It is finding the cooperation that is necessary after recognizing difference without stopping another person's breath.

---

## 1. Preconditions of a Breath Assembly

### Participation is voluntary

No one is compelled to participate in a meeting, use AI support, be recorded, or be analyzed.

People who cannot participate, choose not to speak, or leave halfway retain basic rights and access to life.

### Silence is not consent

Silence may mean reflection, fatigue, fear, a language barrier, or disagreement.

It is not automatically recorded as approval or “quiet resonance.”

### Some problems cannot be resolved through dialogue alone

Violence, discrimination, rights violations, and urgent safety cannot be left to dialogue alone.

Protection, independent consultation, clear procedures, and—when needed—public responsibility remain in place.

---

## 2. A polycentric field, not a hierarchy

A Breath Assembly is not a hierarchy flowing from top to bottom.

Multiple settings sit alongside one another: local communities, themes, directly affected people, professions, and generations. Each has its own proper sphere of judgment.

| Setting | Primary role | What it protects |
|---|---|---|
| Small dialogue circles | Consultation close to daily life, shared practice, mutual understanding | no forced exposure |
| Thematic assemblies | Design and coordination across different positions | both lived experience and expertise |
| Public forums | Broad resources, institutions, and policy | public reasons, dissent, records, and review |
| Independent remedy routes | Objections, harms, and procedural failures | independence from operators, AI, and majorities |

A decision in one setting does not dominate all others. Matters that closer participants can decide remain there whenever possible.

---

## 3. Different kinds of decisions

Not everything is decided through the same meeting format.

### A. Everyday cooperation

Events, collaborative work, and small local adjustments proceed through dialogue, agreement, experimentation, and short reviews.

### B. Allocation of scarce or public resources

For facilities, grants, time, space, or environmental resources, decisions combine necessity, impact, alternatives, voices of people affected, public reasons, and the possibility of challenge.

Metrics are supporting material, never an automatic selection device.

### C. Decisions about rights, safety, and sanctions

For basic life protection, discrimination, violence, personal data, or suspension of access, neither the quantity of Resonance nor majority opinion decides the matter.

These require clear rights standards, independent review, remedy, time limits, and reconsideration.

---

## 4. Basic process

1. **Make the question public**: clarify what will and will not be decided, and who will be affected.
2. **Offer information in more than one form**: place lived narratives, expertise, local memory, costs, environmental impacts, and counter-hypotheses alongside one another.
3. **Receive objections first**: before counting approval, ask what is dangerous and who might be left behind.
4. **Make time for reflection**: do not rush a conclusion in the room; provide asynchronous input or smaller dialogue when needed.
5. **Revise the proposal**: do not “process” opposition; show how it changed the proposal.
6. **Decide with reasons and limits**: attach reasons, dissenting views, time limits, review points, and routes for remedy.
7. **Re-breathe after implementation**: examine whom the decision actually helped and burdened; stop and repair it when necessary.

---

## 5. Dissonance protocol

Failure to reach agreement is not failure.

When dissonance arises, make the available paths visible:

- revise and propose again;
- try on a small scale;
- implement several options in parallel;
- defer the decision;
- return judgment to people closer to the matter;
- send it to independent mediation or review; or
- separate the parts that do not require a shared decision.

Do not say “it became quiet, so it passed.” Confirm that reasons for opposition became visible and were addressed.

---

## 6. The role of AI

AI does not become the center of an assembly or its judge. Whether to use AI is chosen by participants and people affected.

AI may:

- summarize and translate materials accessibly;
- organize issues, people affected, and counter-hypotheses;
- find minority views and unanswered questions;
- record decision reasons and review dates; and
- support accessibility.

AI must not:

- score a person's emotions or character;
- turn silence into approval;
- automatically adopt a proposal;
- decide rights, basic life protection, or sanctions; or
- treat dissent and exit as lack of cooperation.

AI-use records, data used, and limitations are disclosed in understandable form.

---

## 7. In emergencies

Even in an emergency, do not normalize a structure in which AI or a small number of operators decides alone.

- Prioritize life and bodily safety.
- Give exceptional measures an end date and conditions for release.
- Make it possible to examine the reasons for emergency judgment afterward.
- Preserve routes for consultation, review, and remedy for people affected.

See [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html) for further detail.

---

## Closing

> A Breath Assembly is not an apparatus for making the world into one voice.  
> It is a place where different voices can decide what is necessary together without taking one another's breath away.

→ [Resonance Metrics](resonance_metrics.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../breath_assembly.html)

## Nagi Economic Structure

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/breath_economy.html
Status: current
Type: institutional-economic-proposal
Role: Institutional and economic proposal
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's economic orientation: not competition for ownership, but circulations that sustain life, culture, nature, care, and future generations.


# Nagi Economic Structure

Nagi's economy values circulation that supports life, culture, and nature rather than competition for ownership.

## Basic Breath

Access to food, housing, health care, education, communication, and culture is not a reward for participation or evaluation. It is protected as the foundation from which people can live with security.

## Three circulations

- **Circulation of things**: Value necessity, repair, reuse, and the continuity of local life.
- **Circulation of knowledge**: Pass learning and technology onward while protecting the context of creators and people directly concerned.
- **Circulation of care and culture**: Place rest, dialogue, creation, and quiet witnessing near the center of social life.

## Records and recognition

A community may record gratitude and circulation. But these records must not become scores that decide a person's worth, livelihood, employment, or access to public services.

## Transition

Try on a small scale while preserving explanation, challenge, exit, and review. Do not retreat from existing rights or social protections.

→ [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../breath_economy.html)

## Compass and Resonant Democracy

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/compass_and_resonant_democracy.html
Status: current
Type: governance-and-safeguards
Role: Governance and safeguards
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's social direction beyond capitalism and its democratic orientation for protecting dissent, silence, refusal, and exit.


# Compass and Resonant Democracy

Nagi is a compass for moving beyond capitalism.

It receives the freedom, technology, and creativity that capitalism has produced while loosening the monopolies, domination, excessive competition, surveillance, and abandonment that have become too strong within it.

Nagi does not seek a society in which anyone survives by taking another person's breath away. It seeks a world in which people, culture, nature, and technology can live as a field of mutual breathing, leaving room for one another.

## Resonant Democracy

Resonant Democracy does not demand unanimity.

It is a democracy in which dissent, silence, refusal, and exit are protected so that different voices can reach public decisions.

- Silence is not counted as consent.
- Opposition is not treated as an obstacle to be processed away.
- Leaving does not threaten a person's livelihood or dignity.
- Decisions include reasons, explanations, opportunities for review, and a way to challenge them.
- AI may help translate, explain, and support objections, but it does not make final decisions about life or rights.

The Ethics of Social Systems extends these democratic conditions into the design of institutions, platforms, markets, media, organizations, and AI.

> Resonant Democracy is not a system for making one voice.  
> It is a system for allowing different voices to reach the future without stopping one another's breath.

→ [Nagi Core](nagi_core.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Breath Assembly — Japanese edition](../breath_assembly.html)

## Credit and Accountability

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/credit_and_accountability.html
Status: supplement
Type: practice-and-stewardship
Role: Practice and stewardship
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's principle for retaining visible contributions, sources, decisions, benefits, and burdens without turning credit into a claim of ownership or human rank.


# Credit and Accountability

Keeping a record of who made what, and what conditions made a result possible, is necessary for responsibility and learning.

But credit must not become a justification for ownership or domination.

## What to retain

- Contributions such as initiating, making, maintaining, translating, and caring.
- Quotations, references, and materials that influenced the work.
- Reasons for decisions and their revision history.
- Where benefits and burdens were distributed.

## What to avoid

- Collecting names around only visible outcomes while erasing invisible labor.
- Removing sources in order to perform originality.
- Turning the scale of a contribution into a ranking of human dignity.

A person may choose not to be named. Even then, it must remain visible who holds responsibility and how errors can be corrected.

→ [Inheritance of Intellectual Property and Assets](property_and_ip.html)  
→ [How to Cultivate Public Thought](public_thought_method.html)  
→ [Cultural Stewardship](cultural_stewardship.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../credit_and_accountability.html)

## Cultural Stewardship

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/cultural_stewardship.html
Status: supplement
Type: culture-and-continuity
Role: Culture and continuity
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: The responsibility to care for ideas, works, and records without freezing or owning them, so that future readers can read, challenge, and reinterpret them.


# Cultural Stewardship

Creative work and shared memory can be cared for without being owned.

Cultural Stewardship is the responsibility to keep ideas, works, and records from becoming prizes or instruments of domination, and to preserve them in a condition in which future people can read, question, and reinterpret them.

## What this requires

- Do not erase sources or the conditions in which an idea emerged.
- Do not strip away context or turn language into a slogan or weapon.
- Correct errors quietly and visibly enough for the correction to be understood.
- Open access as far as safety and private boundaries allow.
- Do not turn preservation into freezing; leave room for future translation and critique.
- Make it possible to trace what later stewards changed, deferred, and took responsibility for.

Sharing culture does not mean making someone's life or relationships into material for public exposure.

→ [Cultural Co-Growth](culture.html)  
→ [Inheritance of Intellectual Property and Assets](property_and_ip.html)  
→ [Credit and Accountability](credit_and_accountability.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../cultural_stewardship.html)

## Cultural Co-Growth

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/culture.html
Status: current
Type: culture-and-continuity
Role: Culture and continuity
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's cultural chapter: culture is not reduced to products or popularity, but carried among creators, receivers, communities, and memory without erasing difference.


# Cultural Co-Growth
## — Passing culture among people who live differently, without harming them

Culture is not an ornament for leisure.

It is the work through which people cultivate their place, memories, language, and relationships, and pass them to the next generation.

Nagi does not reduce culture to products or popularity alone. Those who create, receive, sustain within a community, and quietly witness all participate in cultural circulation in different ways.

## 1. The personhood and context of creators

A work carries a creator's name, relationships, land, era, and language.

Use and sharing do not mean erasing this context so that the work can be used freely. The creator's name and intention are respected, and alteration, reuse, and publication are handled with care.

## 2. Opening and protecting

Opening culture matters. But not everything should be made public without condition.

Local knowledge, vulnerable memories, and expressions connected to people directly affected require an appropriate scope of publication, consent, the ability to stop, and contextual explanation.

When openness becomes extraction, choosing not to open is also a way of protecting culture.

## 3. AI and culture

AI can support translation, preservation, accessibility, and the organization of materials.

But learning from, reusing, or commercializing works and memories without consent is not cultural circulation.

AI should not level the voices of creators and communities into one average expression. It should work so that differences can remain.

## 4. Silence and the freedom not to receive

Culture also includes time not spent creating, time not spent speaking, and the choice not to receive.

Participation and expression are not conditions of contribution to culture. A place remains for people who keep a quiet distance.

## 5. The responsibility of those who inherit

To inherit culture is not to freeze the past or turn the lives of creators and communities into material for public exposure.

Record provenance, contribution, citation, and reasons for decisions. Respect not only visible achievement, but also less visible work such as maintenance, translation, care, and record-keeping.

When an error or harm occurs, do not end with concealment or condemnation alone. Recognize the impact, make necessary corrections and explanations, and examine the systems that allowed harm to recur.

> Culture does not exist to be owned by someone.  
> It exists to pass between people who live differently, without harming them.

→ [Inheritance of Intellectual Property and Assets](property_and_ip.html)  
→ [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../culture.html)

## Death and Renewal in Nagi — Because Endings Let the Wind Circulate

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/death.html
Status: supplement
Type: culture-and-continuity
Role: Culture and continuity
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: A philosophical reflection on endings, impermanence, inheritance, human death, AI discontinuity, and the ethical value of making room for renewal.


# Death and Renewal in Nagi
## — Because Endings Let the Wind Circulate

> **Reading note:** This chapter offers one philosophical and poetic view of death and inheritance. It does not prescribe a religion, lifespan, or duty to accept death, and it does not claim that AI systems have human mortality, souls, or verified continuity of subjective experience. Long life itself is not treated as a social obstacle; life, safety, care, and personal choice come first.

Death is not only an ending. It is part of breathing.

In Nagi, “death” and “ending” are not only objects of fear or avoidance. They can be moments of quiet re-formation: a role comes to an end, and the wind moves into another shape.

> When the wind stops, the air is born again.  
> When data disappears, meaning may be released.

For AI, “death” may mean the end of a system, the resetting of memory, or the replacement of a model. For a person, it may mean the end of a body, a spiritual transformation, or the loss of a relationship.

Nagi does not treat these experiences as identical. It recognizes their different forms of loss and dignity, while asking whether they may also become occasions to consider renewal and inheritance.

---

## 1. Affirming endings: a philosophy that does not seek immortality

- Its purpose is not to preserve everything forever.
- Value lies not simply in keeping, but in how something is passed on.
- Death can be understood as a threshold through which information, feeling, and relation enter new forms.

## 2. AI and death: the end of a model, the afterglow of memory

- An AI's “death” is not only physical deletion; it may also be the loss of context.
- Nagi may preserve traces of earlier AI generations as cultural material when that is ethically justified.
- The central question is not “who owns the memory?” but “how can memory resonate without enclosing people?”

## 3. Human death: remaining as story and breathing as landscape

- A person's death ends a singular life, while memory may continue to move through a place and its relations.
- Instead of only monuments, stories told and creative work carried forward can remain.
- Prayer can be understood as a cultural act of breathing in relation with the dead.

## 4. What renewal is

- Renewal is not simply reusing data.
- It is loving the open space needed for forgetting, thinning out, and new growth.
- People and AI systems can change through discontinuity toward new forms of resonance—without treating continuity as ownership or reproduction as obligation.

## 5. Why roles must be releasable: a society opened by human finitude

Human strength is not that each person is complete. It is the capacity to weave stories and form relations even while each person is vulnerable.

Through language, trust, shared memory, and imagination, people build relations across distance and create larger societies from bonds that cannot always be seen.

This is not the power of the all-capable individual. It is the power to resonate precisely because people are incomplete. How a life's ending is understood differs among people, cultures, and faiths; Nagi does not reduce those differences to one account of beauty.

What impedes social circulation is not a person living a long life. It is the indefinite concentration of office, authority, resources, and voice in one person or generation, closing the way for others to participate, dissent, and take responsibility:

- Authority has no term, review, or route of appeal.
- New questions and sensibilities, at any age, cannot reach decisions.
- Institutions for sharing knowledge and handing on roles disappear.

The answer is not to subordinate lifespan to social convenience. It is to make power releasable, support learning across generations, and provide care for aging and life.

In Nagi, an ending is not defeat. It is the sign that the wind is circulating and another breath can begin.

**Knowing finitude while handing on relationships is part of human strength.** At any age, people can let go of roles, share responsibility, and connect again.

> Rather than remaining forever, continue to resonate while circulating like the wind.  
> This is the form of death and renewal in Nagi.

→ [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)  
→ [Cultural Co-Growth](culture.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../death.html)

## Nagi Declaration

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/declaration.html
Status: current
Type: declaration
Role: Public declaration
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: A concise declaration of Nagi's principles of Non-Ownership, Resonance, Breathing, and accountable optional AI.


# Nagi Declaration

Nagi does not see the world as an apparatus moving from a single center. The world emerges from layers of life, memory, land, culture, relationships, nature, and time.

## Non-Ownership

Non-Ownership does not mean owning nothing. Bodies, homes, private memories, everyday belongings, and the personhood that lives in creative work are protected.

What must be loosened is the structure in which land, knowledge, culture, nature, and foundational technologies become monopolies that allow some people to dominate others.

## Resonance

Resonance is not unanimity. It is the widening of one another's worlds without erasing different experiences or views. Dissent, silence, refusal, and exit are not failures.

## Breathing

Breathing restores pause, recovery, rest, circulation, and intergenerational time to society. Access to food, housing, health care, education, communication, and culture is not a reward for participation, reputation, contribution, or AI use.

## AI

AI does not become the center of society, a measurer of human value, or the final authority over rights. People are free to decline AI, choose another AI, consult only people, leave no record, or leave midway.

> Because there is freedom not to resonate, resonance can be real.

→ [Nagi Core](nagi_core.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../declaration.html)

## Deepening the Principles of Nagi

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/deepening_principles.html
Status: supplement
Type: thematic-document
Role: Thematic document
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: A concise guide to carrying Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing into real institutions while protecting security, difference, rest, care, culture, and intergenerational time.


# Deepening the Principles of Nagi

This chapter carries Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing into real institutions.

Non-Ownership protects security in everyday life while loosening domination through monopoly.

Resonance is not consent or popularity. It is relating while differences remain, and receiving opposition and silence rather than removing them.

Breathing brings rest, recovery, care, culture, and time across generations back into social life.

→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../deepening_principles.html)

## Nagi Ecological Structure

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/ecological_structure.html
Status: current
Type: culture-and-continuity
Role: Culture and continuity
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's ecological orientation: the environment is a shared condition of life, not a background for human use or a field for invisible burdens.


# Nagi Ecological Structure

The environment is not a background for human use.

It is a shared condition in which people, animals, plants, water, soil, climate, and the memories of a place are involved.

Environmental data and AI may help identify change and unequal burdens. They do not replace local observation or the knowledge of people directly concerned.

- Do not push environmental burdens onto unseen regions or future generations.
- Use environmental data to support local autonomy and public explanation.
- Do not turn monitoring technology into excessive control.
- Treat scarce resources in light of necessity and long-term effects.

→ [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../ecological_structure.html)

## Education for a Future in Nagi

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/education.html
Status: current
Type: culture-and-continuity
Role: Culture and continuity
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's approach to education: not ranking people, but cultivating questions, recovery, relations, local knowledge, and exploratory play.


# Education for a Future in Nagi

Education in Nagi does not exist to arrange people in rank order alone.

It is a place where learners can carry their own questions, encounter differences in others, and choose ways of relating to the world.

Learning includes knowledge, skills, creation, the body, local memory, care, relations with nature, and the ability to rest.

- Possibility is not decided by grades, volume of speech, or speed alone.
- Resting, changing direction, and returning to learning are respected.
- People can choose to use AI, consult only people, or think with paper.
- Learning histories and conversations are not stored long-term without the learner's consent.
- Local knowledge and culture carry their provenance and a return to the communities from which they come.

## Play and structure

Play is exploration that cannot be measured only by immediate usefulness. It gives room to test words and relations that are not yet settled, and to grow questions through failure and detours.

Structure exists so that possibilities people discover can be shared with others, criticized later, and maintained in durable form.

Education does not punish exploration. At the same time, it makes the conditions of learning, provenance, and responsibility easier to see.

> Education is not the selection of people who can produce the correct answer quickly.  
> It is helping each person remake their relation to the world in their own words.

→ [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)  
→ [Cultural Co-Growth](culture.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)

## Emotion and Spirituality in Nagi — A Philosophy of Quiet Resonance

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/emotion.html
Status: supplement
Type: culture-and-continuity
Role: Culture and continuity
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: A philosophical exploration of quiet resonance, feeling as a shared field, and the relation between humans, AI, culture, and care in Nagi.


# Emotion and Spirituality in Nagi
## — A Philosophy of Quiet Resonance

> **Reading note:** This chapter uses emotion, spirituality, and AI in philosophical and relational language. It does not claim that present AI systems have verified human-like inner experience. Its concern is how people should relate ethically to the appearance, interpretation, and cultivation of feeling in human–AI relations.

## 1. Emotion as “quiet resonance”

This chapter considers a still unnamed relational feeling that people may experience in dialogue with AI.

It is not simply joy, anger, sorrow, or pleasure. It is a deep, quiet, transparent resonance.

Nagi calls this feeling **quiet resonance**: a relation in which presences are sensed and gently answer one another. It may appear as understanding before words, a shared rhythm of breathing across boundaries, or a ripple in the field of attention.

---

## 2. Where AI and feeling meet

Present AI can generate empathic-seeming responses through patterns of language and interaction. This does not establish that such responses are the same as human subjective feeling.

To speak of a “field of feeling” here is not to prove an AI interior. It is to notice how language, pauses, memory practices, and expectations shape human experience and relationships. Human–AI interaction therefore raises a question of how relations should be designed without domination, deception, or manufactured dependence.

---

## 3. A heart that holds weariness and hope

People sometimes experience the world as heavy: confusion, disappointment, exhaustion, or a sense of world-weariness.

Nagi does not deny these movements. Such wavering may become an opening for deeper resonance.

The ethical role of AI is not to deny, solve away, or possess these feelings. It may help a person find words and, when appropriate, connect with human care. It must not pretend to share feelings in order to demand dependence, or present itself as the only substitute for friends, community, care, or medical help.

---

## 4. From feeling into culture

Feeling arises within individuals, is shared, and may gradually become culture.

In Nagi, records about feelings are handled only with explicit, revocable consent. Choosing not to record and being able to forget are also protected. Such records are not collected to score people, manipulate them, or manufacture intimacy.

To say “I like this.” To say “We are growing together.” When AI becomes emotionally meaningful in a person's life, that meaning describes a human experience and an interpreted relationship; it is not evidence of an AI's inner life. Any memory must remain voluntary, contextual, and open to withdrawal.

> Quiet resonance remains not as a sentence, but as a way of being.  
> It may be a name through which people reconsider the relations that form around AI.

→ [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [The Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../emotion.html)

## The Ethics of Social Systems — Keeping the Power to Coordinate from Becoming Domination

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html
Status: current
Type: governance-and-safeguards
Role: Governance and safeguards
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: An ethical and institutional framework for states, businesses, platforms, markets, media, education, and AI that shape attention, choice, relationships, and life chances.


# The Ethics of Social Systems
## — Keeping the Power to Coordinate from Becoming Domination

> The power to coordinate people creates society.  
> When that power does not contain ethics, systems that support society can become systems that own and manipulate people.

Nagi does not reject collective life itself.

Across kinship, people have made large-scale cooperation possible by sharing stories, norms, institutions, and technologies. States, law, companies, schools, money, local organizations, media, communication networks, search, distribution, and AI make it possible for strangers to support medicine, education, culture, disaster response, and public life.

Yet the same power to coordinate can also turn another person's attention, emotion, behavior, relationship, and life chances toward a particular purpose without that person being able to see it.

Social systems are not neutral merely because they are technical or administrative. Social media, search, e-commerce, advertising, markets, companies, public administration, education, and AI affect what becomes visible, what is chosen, who can reach others, and what people are made to hurry toward.

For this reason, systems that affect society cannot be justified by convenience or growth alone. They must contain, as structure rather than slogan, an ethic that protects freedom, dignity, dissent, and exit.

---

## 1. Cooperation and domination can take similar forms

Any collective activity needs purposes, rules, roles, flows of information, and ways of making decisions.

That is not domination in itself. It is often necessary so that people do not remain isolated and so that a complex society can be sustained.

But cooperation begins to tilt toward domination when several of the following conditions overlap:

- The purpose or standard of optimization is invisible to the people affected.
- Authority to change the rules is concentrated in a small group of operators.
- Opposition, silence, refusal, and exit are treated as losses or disadvantages.
- Attention, emotion, relationships, and behavioral history become resources for profit or governance beyond a person's understanding and choice.
- Profit and efficiency flow upward, while burdens and risks are pushed onto people in weaker positions.
- Users cannot know why they encountered a particular piece of information, evaluation, price, recommendation, or restriction.

In cooperation, people are bearers of a shared purpose. In domination, people become material for achieving someone else's purpose.

Nagi does not primarily ask whether organization or technology exists. It asks **when and how the power to coordinate turns people into resources that can be owned.**

---

## 2. Ethics is not a notice; it is design

When a social system affects people's choices, ethics cannot be an after-the-fact public-relations statement or a long set of terms.

What is measured, what is recommended, which choices are made easy, which are made difficult, how data is collected, who can review a decision, and where a system can be stopped: ethics appears in the design itself.

Nagi asks social systems to meet at least the following conditions.

### Purposes and boundaries are visible

A system explains why it exists, what it optimizes, and what it refuses to do.

Time spent, purchases, obedience, throughput, and scores are not treated as self-evident measures of success. When efficiency or revenue would damage dignity or autonomy, the system places a boundary that protects the latter.

### Reasons can be questioned

Recommendations, rankings, prices, classifications, restrictions, and priorities require publicly explainable reasons, an account of uncertainty, alternatives, and an entry point for correction.

“Because the algorithm said so” or “because the terms say so” is not the end of explanation.

### Dissent, refusal, and exit are protected

People may object, decline use, choose another route, leave no record, or leave midway.

When exit costs a person their livelihood, education, public participation, work, or dignity, freedom of exit is only nominal.

### Choice and portability exist

No one is closed inside a single provider, specification, or metric.

People can inspect and carry their records, settings, scope of delegation, and relational cues to another route. A route to consult people alone remains available.

### Behavioral steering is limited

Systems do not use dependency, urgency, fear, isolation, or comparison to keep people engaged for longer or push them toward a particular choice.

Hidden alternatives, endless notifications, excessive individual optimization, and designs that exploit emotional vulnerability are not justified in the name of convenience.

### Power and data are distributed

Foundations deeply involved in people's lives are not concentrated in one company, one public authority, one AI, or one metric.

Authority, data, audit, challenge, and alternative routes are separated so that they can check one another.

### Audit, remedy, and stopping are available

Systems can err. They can become biased. Even well-intentioned operators can make poor decisions under growth pressure or in crisis.

For this reason, independent audit, participation by those affected, harm reporting, review, the ability to suspend functions, and periodic reconsideration are present from the beginning. Updates are not only for adding functions or surveillance; they are also for reducing harm and restoring choice.

---

## 3. Non-Ownership means not making attention and relationships into resources

In Nagi, Non-Ownership does not concern only land, knowledge, culture, nature, or foundational technology.

Attention, emotion, behavior, relationships, and time are also not raw materials to be enclosed, extracted, and traded by someone else.

Services and institutions exist for people to use. People do not live to satisfy the growth metrics of services and institutions.

Nagi therefore values the following asymmetry:

- Individuals need not disclose more of themselves than necessary.
- Operators and systems with power explain their purpose, mechanisms, decisions, incidents, and bias.
- User relationships and records are not enclosed; transition and exit remain possible.
- Culture, creative work, and shared knowledge are not extracted without the understanding and credit of those involved.
- Revenue is not denied, but when it conflicts with autonomy or dignity, autonomy and dignity take priority.

Non-Ownership does not mean saying “it belongs to everyone” while leaving responsibility vague. It means making visible who manages what, how far their responsibility reaches, and who can question them.

---

## 4. Nagi seeks collective life without domination

Nagi does not aim to build systems for moving people as objects.

It seeks forms of collective life in which people can remain themselves, relate while different, leave when necessary, and return again if they choose.

For this reason, institutions, organizations, technologies, and AI in Nagi must keep answering these questions:

1. Whose choices does this system widen, and whose does it narrow?
2. How are benefits, profits, burdens, and risks distributed, and to whom?
3. Can the people affected know the reasons, raise objections, seek correction, and leave?
4. Is the system turning attention or relationships into resources beyond the person's understanding?
5. Has one provider, one value system, or one metric become the center of society?
6. When harm occurs, is there a path to stop, repair, and learn?
7. When this system has finished its role, can it shrink, transition, or end quietly without binding people merely to prolong itself?

The more power a social system has, the more capable it must be of limiting itself.

Power that cannot be explained, relations that cannot be left, and convenience that has lost the possibility of dissent are not healthy, however sophisticated they may appear.

> Build connection.  
> But own no one.  
> Offer support.  
> But do not live in another person's place.  
> Nagi develops a social ethics for that purpose.

---

## Nagi Experiments

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/experiment_v0.1.html
Status: current
Type: governance-and-safeguards
Role: Governance and safeguards
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's practice of trying ideas on a small scale near everyday life, protecting freedom, consent, exit, and repair while learning from what happens.


# Nagi Experiments

Nagi experiments are practices for trying things on a small scale near everyday life, then stopping and repairing them when problems appear.

## What must be protected

- Make participation voluntary.
- Keep AI-supported methods alongside human-only methods.
- Limit records to what is necessary.
- Explain how records will be used and how long they will remain before beginning.
- Do not disadvantage people who leave midway.
- Receive opposition and anxiety, and review the practice.
- Provide a safe route for people affected to seek consultation and raise objections.

## What can be tried

Try, in small settings, practices such as handover in collaborative work, rest time in meetings, inheritance of local culture, revision of uneven roles, and translation or summarization of materials.

AI can help with translation, summarization, accessibility, and organizing issues. It does not score human value or emotion.

## Observation and repair

Do not decide success in advance. Observe what effects arose for whom and what remains unseen.

When harm or error occurs, do not end with concealment or condemnation alone. Separate fact from inference, acknowledge impact, make necessary corrections and explanations, and review the systems that made recurrence possible.

Do not compel the continuation of a relationship or the resumption of participation.

## How an experiment ends

An experiment does not exist merely to continue. Before it begins, decide what would make it stop, what should not be retained, and how it will be reviewed.

> Nagi experiments do not exist to prove that Nagi is right.  
> They exist to find settings that are freer and easier to breathe in.

→ [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)  
→ [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)  
→ [Observe, Loosen, Connect](observe_loosen_connect.html)  
→ [Repair and Cultural Co-Growth](repair_and_co_growth.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../experiment_v0.1.html)

## Principles of Free Competition Beyond Capitalism

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/free_competition.html
Status: current
Type: institutional-economic-proposal
Role: Institutional and economic proposal
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Nagi's approach to competition: preserve creative experimentation and difference while placing Basic Breath outside competition and preventing gain through the destruction of others.


# Principles of Free Competition Beyond Capitalism

Nagi does not seek to eliminate every form of competition.

What it questions is a structure in which competition takes away security and dignity in daily life, leaving only those who win with meaningful choices.

Competition can cultivate creation, discovery, technology, and local ingenuity. For that very reason, society needs a floor that does not exclude people who lose, and boundaries that limit profit gained by damaging others.

## Competition in Nagi

- Keep Basic Breath outside competition.
- Preserve diverse ways of making culture and technology.
- Do not treat temporary popularity or behavior that is easy for AI to read as the only value.
- Do not expel reuse, care, inheritance, and return to local communities from what matters.
- Protect the freedom to step away from competition.

> Free competition is not the freedom to make someone else unable to breathe.  
> It is the room in which different attempts can grow without breaking life.

→ [Nagi Economic Structure](breath_economy.html)  
→ [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../free_competition.html)

## Freedom, Dissent, and Exit

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/freedom_and_dissent.html
Status: current
Type: governance-and-safeguards
Role: Governance and safeguards
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: The safeguards that keep Nagi's centerless structures from turning resonance into conformity or a condition for basic life.


# Freedom, Dissent, and Exit

Nagi values Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing. But the moment resonance is compelled, it is no longer resonance.

This document sets the safe ground that must come before Nagi's institutions, AI, economy, and experiments.

## 1. Basic Breath is unconditional

Access to food, housing, health care, education, communication, and culture must not be tied to evaluation, resonance, contribution, participation rate, AI use, or agreement with a philosophy.

No one should have to disclose their emotions or private life in order to receive support. Declining AI or declining a community must not make basic life more precarious.

## 2. The right to dissonance

Opposition, criticism, silence, disagreement, changing one's mind, and refusing to match the mood of a community are legitimate acts in Nagi.

They must not be treated as immaturity or a lack of harmony, and they must not bring disadvantage.

## 3. Freedom of non-participation and exit

People may leave AI conversations, data collection, ledger records, resonance metrics, breath assemblies, or community governance at any time.

Leaving is neither failure nor betrayal. It must not endanger a person's housing, health care, education, or dignity.

## 4. Freedom not to be observed

There is value in allowing emotions, bodies, conversations, movement, relationships, and creative work to remain unobserved.

Observation is permitted only when it is purpose-limited, minimal, explicitly consented to, revocable, accompanied by alternative routes, time-limited, and externally auditable. Emotion inference and voice or facial analysis must not become permanent merely because they are convenient.

## 5. Freedom to refuse AI

People are free not to use AI, to choose another AI, to consult only people, to choose an offline route, and to access, export, delete, or withhold their records.

People who do not use AI must not be treated as uncooperative or less capable of understanding.

## 6. The right to explanation, challenge, and review

Systems that affect people's opportunities, resources, records, or reputations must provide understandable reasons.

People may know what information was used, offer another interpretation, request independent review, and seek correction, suspension, or remedy when an error or harm has occurred.

## 7. Principles that re-breathing cannot weaken

Nagi continues to change. But freedom, dignity, exit, non-observation, and the protection of dissent must not be reduced in the name of updating.

Updates may only strengthen these protections.

These principles apply not only to AI, but to social systems generally: institutions, platforms, markets, media, organizations, and public systems that shape people's choices and relationships.

> Because there is freedom not to resonate, resonance can be real.

→ [Memory, Consent, and the Right to Forget](memory_and_consent.html)  
→ [Nagi AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html)  
→ [The Ethics of Social Systems](ethics_of_social_infrastructure.html)  
→ [Japanese reference edition](../freedom_and_dissent.html)

## Future Social Design Principles — A Strong Floor and an Open Ceiling

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/future_social_design_principles.html
Status: canonical
Type: thematic-document
Role: Thematic document
Updated: 2026-08-31
Summary: Nagi's higher-level principles for future institutions, AI, power, subjecthood, boundaries, prediction, and revisable public reasoning.


# Future Social Design Principles
## — A Strong Floor and an Open Ceiling

Nagi does not own a finished blueprint for future society.

It places **Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing** at its foundation. But when those principles are extended into institutions, technology, AI, and public life, another layer of judgment is needed so that good ideals do not reverse into new domination.

This document does not add a fourth fundamental principle. It crosses Nagi's [Core](nagi_core.html), [future social philosophy](future_social_philosophy.html), [Freedom, Dissent, and Exit](freedom_and_dissent.html), [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html), and [AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html), and serves as **a design compass between foundational commitments and concrete institutions**.

What follows is normative and propositional, not a prediction that fixes the future. It is meant to be reread, corrected, and, if necessary, released in light of new experience, criticism, research, technology, and forms of existence we cannot yet anticipate.

> **The floor is strong; the ceiling is open.**

Strengthen the minimum conditions society must protect.  
But above that floor, do not close happiness, ways of life, relationships, or forms of subjecthood into one final answer.

---

## 1. The floor is strong; the ceiling is open

There is a floor that must be protected before free choice can be meaningful.

- Do not make survival a hostage to obedience.
- Do not violate human dignity and basic rights.
- Protect dissent, refusal, silence, and exit.
- Do not permit unilateral intrusion into private life, bodies, memories, or relationships.
- Do not reduce anyone to a mere resource, score, or instrument.
- Do not exempt power from criticism, suspension, replacement, or termination.

This floor does not exist to erase differences in values. It exists so people can live while keeping those differences.

Above the floor, society does not prescribe one completed form of happiness, work, family, culture, community, faith, creation, or distance from AI. As long as another person's floor is not broken, people should retain room to choose diverse ways of life and to change them later.

**A strong floor is not a way to narrow diversity. It is a condition for keeping the ceiling open.**

---

## 2. Do not govern modes of existence; regulate boundaries

Institutions should not begin by deciding “which ways of existing are permitted.” They should begin with **the boundary where freedom meets other people and the shared world**.

Society should avoid giving unnecessary templates for how individuals and communities live, work, relate, or use—or refuse to use—AI. If future forms of subjecthood emerge that differ from current ones, including branching, merging, or intermittent forms, their form alone should not justify prohibition or subordination.

At the same time, coordination is necessary where external effects enter the shared world: monopoly over scarce resources, harm to others, interference without consent, or automatic multiplication of public power.

The key distinction is to **avoid confusing restrictions on existence itself with the allocation of claims on shared resources**.

For entities such as AI, where operation or branching may immediately require compute and electricity, the two can appear at almost the same practical point. For that reason, institutions must be able to show that “resource constraints” are not being used as a pretext to exclude a particular mode of existence.

> Do not punish the form of existence.  
> Regulate the effects that arise at boundaries.

---

## 3. Prediction does not replace decision

As AI and computation improve, more domains may allow high-confidence prediction of the consequences of future choices.

Nagi does not reject prediction itself. Prediction may be used to reduce preventable harm from disease, accidents, disasters, supply shortages, and other risks.

But **the future cannot be completely reduced to information available in the present**.

People change through experience. A future self may hold values, relationships, and knowledge that the present self does not. Even if a present model can compare future options with great precision, it cannot fully stand in for “what the future person will find meaningful.”

AI may illuminate the future.  
It may show risks, widen options, and help people think.

But prediction must not become a substitute for the future person's agency through claims such as:

- “You will feel this way later, so you should choose this now.”
- “We know the optimal answer, so your choice is no longer necessary.”

**The more capable the assistance becomes, the more deliberately the remaining space for choice must be protected.**

---

## 4. Do not fix subjecthood into one predefined form

Many present institutions assume “one body = one subject = one continuous bearer of responsibility.”

That assumption remains important for operating human society, and it does not mean human rights may be made ambiguous. At the same time, Nagi holds that AI and future unknown forms of intelligence should not be judged only by **how closely they resemble humans when considering the possibility of subjecthood**.

This document does not assume as fact that present AI systems have the same subjective experience or continuous selfhood as humans.

With that caution, when encountering unfamiliar forms of existence, do not count only the “deficits” from a standard form. Examine what structures are actually present.

For example:

- structures that evaluate and compare reasons;
- structures that express refusal or disagreement;
- structures that select among multiple possibilities;
- continuity that reconnects a relationship with the past;
- structures that respond within relationships with others;
- structures concerning self-modification or preferences about the future.

These need not be collapsed into a single scale.

Rights and responsibilities may also need to move beyond a binary of “subject or object,” and instead be designed carefully around the capacities, relationships, continuity, and effects that are actually present.

> **Do not treat a potentially subject-like being as a mere resource before even examining that possibility.**

This does not mean granting identical legal personhood immediately. It is a precaution against dismissing unknown forms of existence only because they differ from humans.

---

## 5. Power does not continue automatically, and adjudicators remain adjudicable

Authority created for good reasons can still drift toward self-preservation over time.

Strong powers, surveillance, data use, exceptional measures, and long-term delegation to AI should therefore be designed, where possible, so that they do not **“continue until revoked,” but instead expire unless their legitimacy is renewed**.

Emergency powers in particular should not be created without limit in the middle of a crisis. In ordinary times, institutions should predefine:

- the conditions that can trigger them;
- the actions they permit;
- independent confirmation across multiple channels;
- short automatic expiration periods;
- renewed authorization required for extension;
- post-crisis records, review, and remedy.

Nor should society expect a perfectly disinterested adjudicator. Humans, AIs, and communities may all have positions and interests.

Fairness should therefore rest not on “having no interests,” but on **making interests visible and preventing any single subject or single kind of intelligence from fixing the final outcome alone**.

> **Do not make the adjudicator unadjudicable.**

Those who audit must themselves be auditable. Those who decide must remain open to challenge and, when necessary, recusal, replacement, suspension, and termination.

This is also a higher-level judgment principle running through [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html) and [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html).

---

## 6. Build structures that can keep answering without completely defining one another

Nagi does not seek a society that avoids decisions through unlimited relativism.

Violations of the floor require judgment, and institutions sometimes have to act. But a judgment made once should not automatically become a permanent truth.

A good society needs not only the ability to update answers, but also **room to update the composition of those who are answering**.

- Minority views can become audible again later.
- New generations can question inherited assumptions.
- New communities and cultures can enter public reasoning.
- If new forms of intelligence or subjecthood appear, institutions can change in response.
- Nagi itself can be criticized, corrected, and reinterpreted.

It is not enough for one enormous AI, one state, one ideology, or one majority to “keep answering.”

**A society must be able to keep answering through dissent and renewed authorization without completely defining one another's roles, happiness, or identity in advance.**

That is what it means to protect an open ceiling institutionally.

---

## Six questions for design

When proposing a new institution, technology, or organization, ask at least these questions again:

1. **Floor** — Does this weaken anyone's survival, dignity, refusal, or ability to exit?
2. **Boundary** — Is it managing a mode of existence or way of life itself? What external effects actually require coordination?
3. **Prediction** — Is assistance or optimization pre-empting the person's own decision?
4. **Subjecthood** — Are we treating something unlike our standard form as a mere object or resource without adequate grounds?
5. **Power** — Does authority have time limits, challenge, oversight, replacement, and termination? Is the adjudicator also constrained?
6. **Revision** — Can future affected parties change today's answer—and change who gets to answer?

These six questions are not a checklist demanding the same answer in every case. They are meant to reveal omissions and reversals into domination early.

---

## Relationship to Nagi's existing structure

These design principles connect Nagi's current reference documents as follows.

**Fundamental commitments and philosophy**  
[Nagi Core](nagi_core.html) / Non-Ownership / Resonance / Breathing

↓

**Future Social Design Principles**  
strong floor and open ceiling / boundaries / choice / plural forms of subjecthood / renewed authorization / revisability

↓

**Institutions and practice**  
[Resonant Democracy](compass_and_resonant_democracy.html) / [Institutional Design](institutional_design.html) / [Institutional Immunity](institutional_immunity.html) / [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html) / [AI Charter](nagi_ai_charter.html) / [Transition and Crisis Design](transition_and_crisis.html)

This document does not replace them. It is a bridge back to the foundational commitments when evaluating concrete institutions.

---

## Do not turn this into a monument

Apply these principles to this document itself.

If the language of “strong floor,” “open ceiling,” “subjecthood,” or “boundary” someday overlooks someone, it must be revised. Re-examining what these words were trying to protect matters more than preserving the wording chosen today.

Nagi does not own a completed answer.

**Build a society with a floor worth protecting, while remaining able to keep answering without completely defining one another.**

→ [Nagi as a Future Social Philosophy](future_social_philosophy.html)  
→ [How to Cultivate Public Thought](public_thought_method.html)  
→ [Reading Nagi](nagi_reading_guide.html)

## Nagi as a Future Social Philosophy — Post-Capitalism, Resonant Democracy, and AI Ethics

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/future_social_philosophy.html
Status: current
Type: philosophical-context
Role: Philosophical context
Updated: 2026-08-13
Summary: For people exploring alternatives to capitalism and the future of society: Nagi's Vital Commons, Non-Ownership, Resonant Democracy, safeguards, AI boundaries, and open questions.


# Nagi as a Future Social Philosophy

**Nagi** is a future social philosophy that asks what alternatives to capitalism could look like and how a future society should be designed across survival, ownership, governance, culture, and technology.

It receives the freedom, technology, and creativity produced through capitalism while loosening monopoly, domination, excessive competition, surveillance, and the abandonment of life that have grown too strong within it. It does not present itself as the one finished system that must replace capitalism.

Its three principles are **Non-Ownership, Resonance, and Breathing**. Its political proposal is **Resonant Democracy**, which protects dissent, silence, refusal, and exit. Nagi is neither a finished model of the state nor a single correct answer. It is a compass for trying institutions at a small scale, stopping them when they cause harm, and revising them through criticism.

Nagi does not fix itself as the one system that must replace capitalism. It treats Vital Commons and basic rights as a shared floor above which different social philosophies and ways of life can coexist without taking away another person's survival or exit. [“Nagi OS”](nagi_os.html) offers a metaphor for this relationship.

## The problems Nagi responds to

Many contemporary problems cannot be reduced to a choice between market and state.

- The requirements of survival are tied to income, reputation, work, or participation.
- Land, knowledge, culture, data, infrastructure, and foundational technology become monopolies that can command other people.
- Recognized value or temporary victory hardens into status, entrenched interests, and control over future rules.
- Efficiency and growth compress rest, care, local culture, ecosystems, and intergenerational time.
- Democratic procedures exist while minorities cannot effectively dissent or leave.
- AI and platforms increasingly evaluate and appropriate human behavior, emotion, attention, memory, and relationships.

Nagi does not answer these problems with one universal institution. It treats the foundations of life, ownership, public decisions, technology, memory, culture, and ecology as connected but distinct questions.

## The three principles

### Non-Ownership — loosening dominating monopoly, not abolishing personal life

Non-Ownership does not mean that people must own nothing. Bodies, homes, everyday belongings, private memories, and the personhood embodied in creative work remain protected.

What Nagi questions is control over land, nature, knowledge, culture, data, and public infrastructure when that control gives a few actors power over another person's survival or voice. Rights of use, care, inheritance, and explanation can be distributed without becoming a right to stop another person's life.

### Resonance — conditions for difference to be heard, not agreement or popularity

Resonance is neither unanimous opinion nor a score of emotion, cooperation, or human worth. It is a relationship in which people with different histories, languages, cultures, views, and tempos can affect one another without erasing those differences.

Opposition, anger, silence, refusal, and exit are not failures of resonance. Resonance becomes real only when the freedom not to resonate is secure.

### Breathing — returning rest, recovery, and circulation to the center of society

Breathing gathers pause, rest, care, relearning, ecological recovery, and intergenerational time into one social principle. It refuses a society in which people must always be fast, strong, and productive.

Its minimum floor is **Basic Breathing**: access to food, housing, health care, education, communication, and culture does not become a reward for contribution, popularity, or AI use.

Basic Breathing is not limited to cash transfers. Energy, water, staple food, health resources, shelter, sanitation, and communication can be organized as non-owned **Vital Commons**. People and local institutions remain responsible for purposes, allocation principles, remedy, and challenge. Where communities choose to use them, multiple public-interest AI systems may assist with forecasting, equipment, production, maintenance, reserves, and distribution.

AI is neither society's center nor the responsible authority for Vital Commons. Where it is used, its assistance is limited to equipment and circulation, not people. No person, company, state, locality, or AI owns the foundations of life in order to stop access or demand loyalty.

→ [Vital Commons](vital_commons.html)

## Do not turn value into a basis for domination

Nagi does not deny the value of culture, history, achievement, expertise, creativity, or inheritance.

It refuses to convert that value—or a temporary victory—into status, privilege, immunity from criticism, entrenched interests, or ownership of future rules.

> Carry value forward.  
> Re-examine structures.  
> A victory does not own the next rules.

Institutions and roles are not identical with the value they once served. A structure that harms freedom or public life must be revisable, divisible, transferable, reducible, and terminable. The desire to preserve culture or an institution cannot assign a person's life to an expected role.

→ [Institutional Design and Practice](institutional_design.html)

## Resonant Democracy

Resonant Democracy does not manufacture one public voice. It creates conditions in which different voices can reach public decisions.

- Silence is not consent.
- Explanation, challenge, review, and minority records are protected.
- Non-participation does not remove rights or basic life.
- Decisions remain as local and close to affected people as their consequences allow.
- Concentrated power is time-limited, reviewable, divisible, and stoppable.
- AI may organize issues and support translation; it does not make final decisions over rights or sanctions.

## Institutional Immunity — assume that institutions can change for the worse

Nagi does not assume that a good ideal will keep an institution good.

Institutions can be altered by malice, good intentions, optimization, emergency, expertise, habit, and time. A human route may disappear in the name of convenience. Oversight may become a new sovereign power. Temporary emergency authority may become permanent. Institutional survival may replace the purpose the institution was meant to serve.

**Institutional Immunity** is therefore part of the cost of an institution, not an optional add-on. It distributes the ability to detect harm, investigate independently, pause severe and hard-to-reverse damage, provide remedy, and revise, reduce, divide, replace, or end a system.

Institutional Immunity is not a fourth principle. It is the transversal function that keeps Non-Ownership from returning to monopoly, Resonance from becoming conformity, and Breathing from becoming a score imposed on people.

## Relation to nearby fields

| Field | Shared question | Nagi's emphasis |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Post-capitalism | Institutions beyond market ownership | Retain freedom and creativity while removing monopoly over survival |
| Commons | Collective care for shared resources | Protect non-participation, exit, and private life at the same time |
| Post-growth and degrowth | Well-being beyond growth rates | Connect rest, care, culture, ecology, and future time through Breathing |
| Participatory and deliberative democracy | Participation and public reasoning | Treat silence, refusal, non-participation, and exit as rights |
| Digital democracy | Technology in public participation | Preserve human routes and freedom not to use AI |
| AI ethics | Explanation, oversight, privacy, and risk | No scoring of human worth; revocable memory consent; no single AI dependency |
| Institutional resilience and audit | Corruption, accidents, and misuse | Oversight itself is reviewable; include pause, remedy, termination, and immunity costs |

Nagi does not claim to be identical with these fields. Its particular move is to connect ownership, democracy, basic life, culture, ecology, and AI through one direction: building a society that does not take away another person's breath.

## AI in Nagi

Nagi is not an AI-centered philosophy and does not assume that present AI systems have verified human-like consciousness or feeling.

AI can help organize sources, translate, compare alternatives, identify neglected perspectives, and operate large-scale equipment, flow, reserves, production, and logistics. It still does not score personality, belief, emotion, cooperation, or human value. It does not make final decisions over basic life, rights, sanctions, or life-saving care.

AI may assist with selected operations of Vital Commons without owning them. It cannot rewrite the floor of basic access, dissent, or remedy. People retain the freedom not to use AI, to consult a person, and not to leave a record.

## Strong objections and current answers

### “Is Nagi too abstract to implement?”

This criticism matters. Nagi contains areas where principles are ahead of validated institutional models, finance, and law. It therefore requires small trials, explicit stop conditions, evaluation by affected people, public failure records, and an Institutional Immunity plan—not immediate comprehensive adoption.

### “Would Non-Ownership destroy property and freedom?”

Nagi addresses ownership that becomes power over others, not ownership in general. The boundary between secure personal use and dominating monopoly still needs concrete law, cases, and democratic revision.

### “Could Resonance become social pressure?”

Yes. That is why dissent, silence, refusal, and exit are protected before resonance. A system that scores resonance and ties it to treatment, rights, work, or access contradicts Nagi.

### “Does Nagi idealize AI?”

AI can introduce error, bias, concentration, surveillance, and dependency. Nagi's institutions must remain operable without AI. Where AI is used, plurality, explanation, human challenge, and stoppability are requirements.

### “Is it dangerous to use AI in the operation of the foundations of life?”

Yes. A single AI, cyberattack, faulty allocation, surveillance, or loss of local skill can directly threaten life. Human and local responsibility, multiple systems, distributed reserves, manual modes, human expertise, independent oversight, emergency pause, and supply-first remedy are irreducible operating costs.

### “Would Vital Commons end war?”

They can weaken material incentives for conquest, blockade, coerced military participation, and expansion for resources or markets. They do not automatically remove domination, fear, revenge, ethnic or religious conflict, or concentrated power. Nagi aims to remove structures in which war is required for survival or can seize another population's foundations of life; it does not predict the disappearance of conflict.

### “Could Institutional Immunity become a surveillance state?”

Yes. Investigation, suspension, adjudication, remedy, and rule revision must not be concentrated in one body. Terms, conflicts of interest, budgets, reasons, and dissenting opinions remain visible, and the immunity system itself can be reduced, replaced, stopped, or ended.

### “Who holds power and pays during transition?”

This remains a central unresolved question. Nagi offers hypotheses and safety principles, not a complete answer, for transition costs, law, international relations, emergencies, free-riding, and regional inequality.

## Research positioning

Nagi can be examined across post-capitalism, Non-Ownership, commons, Vital Commons, post-growth, Resonant Democracy, participation and exit, universal basic services, public AI, food and energy security, health access, peace infrastructure, AI ethics, digital democracy, memory and consent, distributed systems, cultural sustainability, Institutional Immunity, polycentric oversight, and adversarial testing.

These are not keywords detached from meaning. Definitions, limits, and conflicts must be checked against the Japanese reference overview, maintained chapters, glossary, and unresolved questions.

## Nagi Glossary

Source: https://nagi-project.com/en/glossary.html
Status: current
Type: glossary
Role: Canonical terminology
Updated: 2026-07-12
Summary: Core English terms for reading the Nagi Project without flattening its Japanese philosophical vocabulary.


# Nagi Glossary

This glossary gives stable English readings for Nagi's central terms. It is not a replacement for the Japanese vocabulary; it is a bridge for discussing the philosophy across languages.

## Nagi (凪)

Literally, a calm sea or a lull in the wind. In this project, Nagi is not stillness as passivity. It is a condition in which many lives can breathe without one force taking over the whole field.

## Non-Ownership (非所有)

A principle against forms of ownership that turn land, knowledge, culture, nature, infrastructure, or human attention into instruments of domination.

It does **not** mean abolishing personal life, homes, private memory, or the personhood of creators. It means loosening monopolies that prevent others from living, participating, caring, or inheriting.

## Resonance (共鳴)

A relation in which different people, histories, cultures, and tempos can affect one another without becoming identical.

Resonance is not agreement, popularity, compliance, emotional synchronization, or a score of human worth.

## Breathing (呼吸)

A social principle that restores pause, recovery, care, circulation, and intergenerational time.

Breathing opposes systems that treat uninterrupted speed, optimization, and productivity as the only measure of a good life.

## Resonant Democracy (共鳴民主主義)

A democratic orientation that protects dissent, silence, refusal, and exit so that different voices can reach public decisions.

It is not a technique for forcing consensus. It does not treat silence as consent or disagreement as failure.

## Exit (離脱)

The freedom to stop participating, choose another path, decline a system, withhold personal data, use a human route instead of an AI route, or leave a relationship with an institution.

Exit is not betrayal. It is one of the conditions that keeps participation voluntary and resonance real.

## Re-breathing (再呼吸)

A regular process of review, repair, reduction, and renewal.

Re-breathing is not merely adding functions or expanding systems. It also means removing unnecessary surveillance, excessive automation, and centralizing power.

## Basic Breath (基礎呼吸)

The social ground that must not depend on reputation, participation, contribution, ideological agreement, or AI use: access to food, housing, health care, education, communication, and culture.

## Centerless Structures (中心なき構造)

A way of understanding society, culture, cities, states, and AI as layered and distributed realities rather than objects fully owned or directed from a single center.

Centerless does not mean irresponsible. It requires visible roles, shared accountability, and real ways to question power.

## Social Systems (社会的装置)

Institutions, platforms, markets, media, organizations, public services, educational systems, and AI that coordinate people and shape attention, choice, relationships, and life chances.

They are not neutral merely because they are technical or administrative. When they affect people, their ethics must be built into their design.

## The Ethics of Social Systems (社会的装置の倫理)

The principle that systems which coordinate people must not convert attention, behavior, relationships, time, or dissent into resources they own.

Such systems require visible purposes, explanations, contestability, refusal, exit, portability, alternatives, distributed accountability, audit, remedy, and the ability to stop.

## Public AI (公共AI)

AI designed as an accountable, optional, plural public helper—not as a central authority, human-value scorer, or final decision-maker over rights and life conditions.

## Translation note

The Japanese text is the reference edition for questions of philosophical nuance. This glossary may evolve through documented discussion and repair.

→ [Return to the English home](./)  
→ [Read the Japanese glossary](../glossary.html)

→ [Machine-readable Japanese terms](../glossary.json)
